awd_titl_txt: Travel: NSF Student Travel Grant for 2025 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR)
awd_abstract_narration:
This award provides partial travel support for students from U.S. institutions to attend the Doctoral Consortium at the 2025 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), taking place in Nashville, Tennessee, from June 11 to June 15, 2025. As the premier international conference in computer vision, CVPR attracts over 10,000 participants annually, showcasing advancements in artificial intelligence, machine learning, and image analysis. The Doctoral Consortium provides a dedicated platform for Ph.D. students to present their research, engage in deep discussions with senior scholars, and receive valuable mentorship to support their career development. By funding travel for approximately 25 students from a wide range of U.S. academic institutions, this award helps nurture the next generation of researchers and broadens participation in a leading technical community.

Selected students will take part in structured consortium activities, including poster sessions, mentorship groups, and career-focused discussions. The travel awards will help cover expenses such as airfare, lodging, and local transportation, ensuring that talented students—especially those with limited financial resources—can attend. Recipients will be chosen by the 2025 CVPR Doctoral Consortium chairs based on research potential, alignment with the conference themes, and the impact of participation on their academic and professional growth.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The NSF Grant supported the 2025 Doctoral Consortium at the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), held in Nashville, Tennessee. CVPR is the premier annual conference in computer vision and a major international forum for research at the intersection of computer vision, machine learning, and artificial intelligence. The conference brings together researchers from academia, industry, and government to present new technical advances, exchange ideas, and build professional networks across areas such as generative AI, robotics, autonomous systems, medical imaging, remote sensing, security, and visual understanding. In addition to the main technical program, CVPR hosts tutorials, workshops, panels, and community events designed to broaden participation and support professional development. The Doctoral Consortium is one such event, providing advanced doctoral students and recent PhD graduates with structured opportunities to present their research, receive feedback, and engage directly with senior researchers in the field.

The 2025 Doctoral Consortium was held in person during CVPR 2025 at the Music City Center in Nashville. The event was highly competitive: 231 students applied, and 36 participants were selected based on their research statements, stage of doctoral study, and potential to benefit from the mentoring experience. NSF support provided travel assistance for 18 students, helping reduce the financial barriers associated with attending a major international conference. The award was led by PI Abby Stylianou.

The event combined research presentations, informal discussion, and structured mentorship. Participants presented their work in a poster session where they received feedback from senior researchers and peers. Students were also matched with mentors whose expertise aligned with their research interests or career goals, enabling more personalized conversations about research direction, career planning, publication strategy, and the transition from doctoral study into academic, industry, or postdoctoral roles. The event also included opportunities for participants to hear broader career advice from experienced members of the CVPR community and to build connections with other early-career researchers.

Feedback from participants indicated that the Doctoral Consortium provided both practical and personal value. Students reported that mentor expertise was generally well matched to their research areas and that the poster session provided useful feedback on their work. Several participants noted that the event increased the visibility of their research within the broader CVPR community and helped them form new professional connections. Written feedback emphasized the importance of access to senior researchers outside one’s home institution, the value of hearing candid advice from established members of the field, and the benefit of meeting peers facing similar research and career transitions. One participant described the event as helping them reflect more clearly on their research direction and feel more confident about the next stage of their career, while another noted that conversations at the consortium helped them navigate a difficult post-PhD job transition and identify a career path that allowed them to continue research closely connected to their doctoral work.

The Doctoral Consortium therefore served as an important professional-development opportunity for emerging computer vision researchers. By enabling students to attend CVPR, present their work, receive individualized feedback, and build networks beyond their own institutions, the NSF travel award helped support the next generation of researchers in computer vision and AI. The event strengthened students’ integration into the broader research community and contributed to the development of future leaders whose work will shape the direction of the field.
